Senses.Explanation: The effort is not spent in vain certifies that an action, answer, or blow has found its mark, often with an immediate warning against turning that certification into merit. After giving both the ritual image and the other one a ladle of foul water, Denghu says the effort is not wasted. When the questioner thanks him for pointing, Guizong replies that the effort is not spent in vain. Yangqi says understanding makes the effort not vain; otherwise an even higher peak remains. An unnamed monk concludes “then the effort is not wasted”; the named headword utterer answers that even vast powers still receive his staff.

Senses.Explanation: A named five-part Caodong sequence concerning achievement and position. The retained five verses begin respectively with the sacred ruler bending the dragon waist; washing off heavy makeup; a withered tree flowering beyond the age; beings and buddhas not encroaching on one another; and horns scarcely grown before they are already unbearable. Senses.Explanation: Awakening is the coming-to-understand that Zen records contrast with delusion and test by what changes in the awakened person's words and conduct. Huineng contrasts being delivered by Hongren while deluded with delivering oneself once awakened. Huangbo Xiyun says awakening lies in the mind rather than in the six perfections, while Kongyin Daodu says it can be in an instant and Dahui Zonggao places it within a finger-snap. Tianran Hanshi says awakening here leaves one free, yet the records do not let the word certify itself: Yongjue Yuanxian asks what two students awakened to, Guting Shanjian warns that wanting to inquire and awaken is incompatible with indulging body and mind, and Miyun Yuanwu can say that the Way does not need awakening. The term therefore names a decisive understanding while remaining answerable to public examination rather than serving as a certificate on its own.

Senses.Explanation: A verb phrase: “awaken” plus “the Way.” Chan records use it retrospectively in biographies and cases: Lingyun awakens on seeing peach blossoms, the Buddha on seeing the morning star, and other monks after an encounter or event; verses composed afterward are called “verses on awakening to the Way.” The stock pairing “awaken to the Way on hearing a sound; clarify mind on seeing a form” is itself raised and questioned in a hall address. The records also police the designation: one text calls memorizing two convenient sayings and naming that “awakening to the Way” one of the enumerated kinds of foolish Chan. Thus the term names an attested event and biographical verdict, while the corpus also records challenges to loose claims of it.

Senses.Explanation: A solitary buddha (pratyekabuddha) is a named class of awakened figure placed beside hearers, bodhisattvas, and buddhas in the records. The witnesses use the figure in ranked lists, scripture quotations raised inside Chan records, and masters’ contrasts; they do not supply an independent life story. Dahui compares the merit of solitary-buddha attainment with the first arousal of resolve, while Huangbo includes attaining the solitary-buddha fruit in a warning about attachment to meritorious roots. Zen bends the inherited category by putting it to work in live appraisal and contrast. The entry does not infer that every solitary buddha teaches, refuses to teach, or belongs to the ancestral lineage.
